What are pygmy sundews?

Pygmy sundews are a group of tiny Australian Drosera, most of them forming rosettes a centimetre or two across. They are grown in a sandy peat mix, kept damp in a tray, and given very strong light, which brings out intense red colour. Despite the size they are tough and fast, and they reproduce by making gemmae in winter. A good pygmy pot can hold dozens of plants and looks like a miniature landscape.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
what are gemmae

Gemmae are small vegetative buds that pygmy sundews produce in the centre of the rosette during the short days of autumn and winter. Each one is a complete clone of the parent, and a single plant can throw dozens. You scrape them off and scatter them on damp sandy peat, where they root and grow into new plants within a few weeks. It is by far the easiest way to multiply pygmies.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How do I harvest and sow gemmae?

Wait until the gemmae sit loose in the crown, usually midwinter, then flick them out with a toothpick or the tip of a knife into a dry container. Scatter them on the surface of damp sandy peat and do not bury them - they need light. Keep the pot in a tray of mineral-free water under bright light, and you should see tiny rosettes within two or three weeks. Sow them promptly, since they dry out and die within days.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Do pygmy sundews need dormancy?

Not a cold dormancy in the way a flytrap does. What they respond to is day length - short days trigger gemmae production instead of flowering, and growth slows a little. Keep them growing through winter with the same light and damp tray, just expect gemmae rather than expansion. A cool but frost-free winter suits most species, and many are quite tolerant of light frost if grown outdoors in a mild climate.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
My pygmy sundew has a weird white tuft in the middle instead of dew.

That is almost certainly gemmae forming, and it is a sign of a healthy plant responding to shortening days. The crown packs with small scale-like buds that look pale and dry compared with the dewy leaves around them. Harvest them and sow them on damp sandy peat if you want more plants, or leave them, in which case they will scatter around the pot and sprout on their own.

What is a tuberous sundew?

Tuberous sundews are Australian Drosera that grow from an underground tuber during the cool wet season and then die back completely to that tuber for a hot dry summer dormancy. Above ground they can be rosettes, erect stems or climbers, depending on species. They are a step up in difficulty, mainly because the summer rest has to be genuinely dry, which is the opposite of everything else in a carnivorous plant collection.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How do I look after a tuberous sundew over summer?

Once the foliage yellows and dies back in late spring, stop watering altogether and let the pot go completely dry. Keep it somewhere warm and out of the rain for the whole summer - this dry rest is what the tuber requires, and keeping it damp will rot it. In autumn start watering again and the plant will emerge on its own. Do not repot or dig around during dormancy unless you are deliberately checking the tuber.

Tell me about Drosera regia.

Drosera regia is the king sundew from South Africa, with strap-like leaves that can reach 40 cm or more on a mature plant. It wants strong light, cool to moderate temperatures, and a very open mix - more sand and perlite than peat - because it dislikes stagnant, heavy soil. It is fussier than a Cape sundew and resents root disturbance. Propagation is easiest from root cuttings, which it takes readily.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Why is D. regia considered difficult?

Mostly because it dislikes heat and heavy soil. It comes from a cool mountain habitat, so prolonged high temperatures stress it, and a dense waterlogged peat mix leads to root problems where a Cape sundew would shrug it off. It also sulks badly after repotting and can take months to recover. Give it an airy sandy mix, mineral-free water, strong light, and cool nights, and leave it alone.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What are the petiolaris complex sundews?

They are tropical Australian sundews from the far north, including species like D. petiolaris, D. lanata and D. falconeri, often with woolly or hairy leaves. Unlike almost everything else in the hobby they want heat - daytime temperatures well above 30 degrees Celsius - along with strong light and high humidity. They are grown in a sandy mix and kept warm year round, which usually means a terrarium or a heated grow chamber.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Can I grow petiolaris sundews on a windowsill?

Rarely successfully. They need sustained high heat and strong light together, and a normal room is far too cool for them even if the window is bright. Most growers use a terrarium or grow chamber with a heat source and a strong light, holding daytime temperatures above 30 degrees. If you want a sundew for a windowsill, a Cape sundew or a D. spatulata is a far better match.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What is an annual sundew?

Annual sundews, like Drosera burmannii and D. sessilifolia, complete their whole life in a single growing season - they germinate, grow fast, flower heavily, set a lot of seed and die. That is not a failure of your care, it is the plan. The way to keep them is to let them seed into the pot, or collect the seed and sow it, so a new generation replaces the old one each year.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
My D. burmannii flowered and then died. Did I do something wrong?

No, that is the normal life cycle - D. burmannii is an annual, so flowering and setting seed is the end of its life. The plant will usually have scattered seed around the pot already. Keep the pot damp and lit as usual and you should see seedlings appear within weeks. If you want to be sure, collect the tiny black seed from the spent stalks and sow it on the surface of damp peat.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How fast does D. burmannii grow?

Very fast by sundew standards - it is one of the quickest, going from seed to a flowering rosette in a couple of months under good light. It also colours intensely red in strong sun and has the fastest leaf movement of the common sundews, wrapping around prey visibly within an hour or two. That speed is exactly why it is a satisfying species to grow from seed.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Tell me about Drosera capillaris.

D. capillaris is a small North American rosette sundew from the southeastern bogs, easy and undemanding. Grow it in a peat and sand mix, kept wet in a tray, in full sun where it takes on strong red colour. In its native range it experiences cool winters and slows down, so a cool rest suits it, but it does not form a tight hibernaculum the way the more northern species do.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How do I grow Drosera intermedia?

Treat it like a temperate bog plant: a peat and sand mix, standing in mineral-free water, in full sun. It tolerates being quite wet, more so than most sundews, and it does well in an outdoor mini bog. It is temperate, so it needs a cool winter rest and will form a small resting bud. Outdoors in a mild temperate climate it can stay out all year with the pot protected from deep freezing.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What is Drosera anglica like to grow?

D. anglica is the English sundew, a temperate species with long upright spoon-shaped leaves. It wants cool conditions, constant moisture, full sun and a genuine winter dormancy, during which it dies back to a hibernaculum. It resents prolonged heat, so summer in a hot climate is the risky season rather than winter. A peat and sand mix or live sphagnum both work well.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
whats a hibernaculum on a sundew

It is the tight bud of curled, dewless leaves that temperate sundews form for winter, once the growing leaves have died back. It looks like a small green or brown knot sitting at soil level and is easy to mistake for a dead plant. Keep the pot damp and cold through winter, do not pull the bud about, and it will unfurl into new growth in spring.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Which sundews stay evergreen all year?

The subtropical ones - Cape sundew, D. spatulata, D. aliciae, D. adelae and their relatives - keep growing through winter as long as you keep the light and warmth up. They benefit from a slightly cooler, slower winter but never die back or form a resting bud. That is exactly why they are recommended for indoor growing, where imposing a real cold dormancy is awkward.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Is Drosera filiformis hard to grow?

Not hard, but it is firmly temperate, so it needs a cold winter and forms a hibernaculum. Through the growing season it makes tall thread-like leaves standing up to 30 cm, covered in dew, and it catches an impressive amount. Grow it in peat and sand, standing in water, in full sun. It is a natural for an outdoor mini bog in a temperate climate.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Tell me about Drosera binata varieties.

D. binata is the forked sundew, and the forms differ mainly in how many times the leaf divides - the simple form splits once into a Y, while multifida and the dichotoma forms fork repeatedly into many points. All want a peat and sand mix, wet feet and strong light. They are temperate to subtropical depending on origin, so many benefit from a cool winter rest but do not always die back fully.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Why does my D. binata die back every winter?

That is normal for the temperate forms - they slow right down and can lose most of their foliage in cold, short days, resprouting from the roots in spring. Keep the pot damp and cool through winter and do not throw it out. If you would rather it kept growing, provide warmth and 14 hours of light, though a rest generally makes for a stronger plant the following year.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What is Drosera prolifera?

D. prolifera is a small Australian rainforest sundew that spreads by producing plantlets on the ends of its flower stalks, which root wherever they touch damp moss. It wants shade rather than blazing sun, high humidity and cool to moderate warmth, so it is very much a terrarium plant. Grow it on live sphagnum kept constantly moist with mineral-free water.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How do I grow Drosera schizandra?

D. schizandra is one of the trickier Queensland species - broad paddle-shaped leaves, low light requirements, constant high humidity and cool stable temperatures. It hates drying out even briefly and hates being too warm. A shaded terrarium on live sphagnum, watered with mineral-free water, is the usual setup. It is not a beginner plant, and most losses come from letting the humidity or moisture swing.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Whats the difference between D. adelae, prolifera and schizandra?

They are the three Queensland sisters, all shade and humidity lovers rather than sun plants. D. adelae has long narrow spear-shaped leaves and spreads aggressively by root suckers, making it much the easiest. D. prolifera is small and spreads by plantlets on its flower stalks. D. schizandra has broad rounded leaves and is the fussiest about warmth and constant moisture.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Which sundews can take full outdoor sun?

Most of the temperate and subtropical rosette and stem species - Cape sundew, D. spatulata, D. capillaris, D. intermedia, D. filiformis, D. binata and the pygmies - colour up beautifully in full sun given wet roots. The exceptions are the Queensland shade species like D. adelae and D. schizandra, which scorch, and the petiolaris complex, which want sun but also more heat than most climates provide.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How do I sow sundew seed?

Scatter it thinly on the surface of a damp peat and sand mix and do not cover it - most sundew seed needs light to germinate. Stand the pot in mineral-free water, keep it bright and warm, and cover with a clear lid or bag for the first weeks to hold humidity. Subtropical species come up in two to four weeks; temperate species usually need several weeks of cold stratification first.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Do sundew seeds need stratification?

It depends on origin. Temperate species like D. filiformis, D. anglica and D. rotundifolia need a cold moist period of about four to six weeks in the fridge before they will germinate. Subtropical and tropical species - Cape sundew, D. spatulata, D. burmannii, the petiolaris complex - need none at all and germinate on warmth and light alone. Sow the sown pot cold if you are unsure of a temperate species.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How long does sundew seed stay viable?

A year or two if kept cool and dry, though germination rates drop noticeably after the first year. Pygmy sundew gemmae are the opposite extreme and last only days, so they must be sown fresh. Store seed in a paper envelope somewhere cool rather than in a sealed bag, and label it with the species and date, because unlabelled sundew seed is impossible to tell apart.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Can I grow sundews in live sphagnum instead of peat?

Yes, and many of the shade and humidity loving species do better in it - D. adelae, prolifera, schizandra and D. regia all appreciate the airiness. Use live or long fibre sphagnum on its own, kept moist with mineral-free water. The one caution is that vigorous live sphagnum can grow up and bury small plants, so trim it back around pygmies and seedlings.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Why do the leaves on my D. adelae have no dew but it keeps growing?

D. adelae is a shade plant, and it produces less dew than a sun-grown rosette sundew even when perfectly happy. Dew also drops off if the air is dry or the plant was recently disturbed. Since it is still growing, the plant is fine. Raise humidity, keep the soil consistently wet with mineral-free water, and accept that this species is never as glittery as a Cape sundew.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
My D. adelae keeps popping up all over the pot.

That is its habit - D. adelae spreads aggressively by root suckers, so a single plant becomes a thicket, and stray roots will send up new plants in neighbouring pots too. It is the easiest sundew to propagate for exactly this reason. If the pot is crowded, tip it out in spring, tease the clump apart and pot up divisions individually.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How do I take a sundew root cutting?

Tip the plant out, snip a few healthy roots into pieces two to four centimetres long, and lay them on the surface of damp peat or sphagnum or bury them barely. Keep the pot humid, bright and warm, and small plantlets appear from the root pieces over the following weeks. It works particularly well for D. capensis, D. binata, D. adelae and D. regia, which have thick roots.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Which sundews are best for a terrarium?

The shade and humidity lovers: D. adelae, D. prolifera and D. schizandra are practically made for one, and the petiolaris complex works if you can supply heat as well. Avoid putting sun-loving species like Cape sundew or the pygmies in a closed case with weak lighting - they stretch and lose colour. A terrarium is a tool for species that want humidity, not a default home.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Do sundews close their leaves quickly?

It varies a lot by species. D. burmannii and the pygmy sundews can visibly curl a leaf margin around prey within an hour, while a Cape sundew takes several hours to bend a leaf right over and the broad-leaved Queensland species barely move at all. All of them digest the same way regardless; movement just concentrates the digestive glands on the catch.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Why has my Cape sundew stopped making dew since I moved it?

Dew production drops when humidity falls, when light drops, or when the plant is stressed by a move, and a new spot usually changes more than one of those at once. Check the light is at least as strong as before, keep the pot standing in mineral-free water, and give it two or three weeks. New leaves emerging with dew is the sign that it has settled.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Can I grow sundews outdoors year round?

Temperate species yes, in a temperate climate - D. filiformis, D. intermedia, D. anglica and D. rotundifolia all overwinter outside in a bog planter given some protection from the pot freezing solid. Subtropical species like Cape sundew survive light frost at best and are usually brought in. Tropical species must come indoors. Match the species to your winter rather than trying to protect the wrong plant.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What sundew would you suggest after Cape sundew?

D. spatulata or D. aliciae if you want more of the same easy rosette habit, D. binata if you want something structurally different with impressive forked leaves, or a pot of pygmies if you fancy the gemmae propagation game. All are straightforward. Leave D. regia, the petiolaris complex and D. schizandra until you have a stable setup, since those need specific temperatures.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Are sundews from seed slower than cuttings?

Yes, considerably. A leaf or root cutting of a Cape sundew gives you a decent plant in a few months, while seed takes closer to a year to reach the same size. Seed is worth it when you want many plants at once, when you want genetic variety, or for annuals like D. burmannii where it is the only option. For quick numbers of one clone, take cuttings.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
My pygmy sundews died back to nothing in summer. Why?

Heat is the usual culprit - many pygmy species come from a Mediterranean climate and struggle when temperatures stay high, especially with poor air movement. Some also naturally slow right down in high summer. Keep them damp and shaded from the worst afternoon heat, and check whether the gemmae you sowed in winter are still coming through, since a fresh generation often carries the pot.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Do pygmy sundews have deep roots?

Surprisingly, yes - pygmy sundews send a single wiry root far deeper than their size suggests, which is why they want a tall pot rather than a shallow one. It is also why they resent being dug up and moved. Sow gemmae directly into the pot you intend to keep them in, and use a pot at least 10 cm deep with a sandy peat mix.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What mix do pygmy sundews want?

Sandier than usual - roughly equal parts peat and washed silica sand, or peat with a good proportion of sand and perlite. They need the drainage but still want the pot standing in a shallow tray of mineral-free water. Use a deep pot to accommodate their long tap root, and top the surface with a thin sand layer, which helps gemmae settle and root.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Is Drosera rotundifolia worth growing indoors?

Not really. It is a cold temperate species that needs a genuine winter dormancy with real cold, and indoor conditions rarely provide that, so plants tend to dwindle over a year or two. It is a lovely plant for an outdoor bog planter in a temperate climate. For indoors, pick a subtropical species like D. spatulata or Cape sundew that grows year round.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How do I overwinter temperate sundews in pots?

Let them form their hibernacula naturally as the days shorten, then keep the pots cold, damp and outside somewhere sheltered - a cold frame, an unheated porch, or sunk into the ground with mulch around them. The aim is cold without the root ball freezing solid for weeks. Water sparingly, just enough that the medium never dries, and resist poking at the buds.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Do sundews need feeding if they never catch anything?

They will survive on light alone but grow slowly and stay small. Indoors, where there is little prey, a few dried bloodworms rehydrated in mineral-free water and placed on the dewy leaves every couple of weeks in the growing season makes a visible difference. Never put fertiliser in the soil, and never use meat from the kitchen - it rots and kills the leaf.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How do I feed a pygmy sundew? The leaves are tiny.

Use crushed dried bloodworm, a very small amount rehydrated into a paste, and place a speck on one or two leaves with a toothpick. The scale is unforgiving, so less is genuinely more - an oversized lump will just rot on the rosette. Feed a few plants in a pot rather than every plant, once every couple of weeks in the growing season.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Whats the tallest sundew I can grow?

D. regia is the giant of the genus, with strap leaves reaching 40 cm or more, though it wants cool conditions and an open mix. For something easier at a decent size, D. binata multifida forms big clumps with tall forked leaves, and D. filiformis sends up thread-like leaves to 30 cm. Climbing tuberous species get taller still but need the dry summer dormancy.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Why do my sundew leaves have dew but nothing sticks to them?

Usually because there is nothing flying about. Indoors, a sundew may go weeks without catching anything simply through lack of insects, which is normal and not a sign of poor dew quality. If you can see plenty of small flies in the room and still nothing sticks, check that the dew droplets are genuinely sticky rather than plain condensation from an over-humid case.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Can I mix different sundew species in one pot?

You can if their needs match - several subtropical rosette species share a pot happily, and pygmies grow well as a mixed carpet. The problem is vigour, not compatibility: D. adelae and D. capensis both self-sow and sucker so aggressively that they smother slower neighbours within a season. Keep the thugs on their own and combine only species of similar speed.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
My sundew is producing flower stalks constantly. Should I keep cutting them?

For a young plant you are trying to grow on, yes - cutting the stalk early puts the energy back into leaves. Cape sundew in particular flowers relentlessly and self-pollinates, so leaving stalks means seedlings in every neighbouring pot. Let one stalk mature if you actually want seed. On a mature, well grown plant flowering does little harm either way.
